q.q: Which best describes the purpose of the CPU?
o: To store files and programs when the power is off
To display the output of programs on the screen
To process data and execute program instructions
To connect the computer to other computers
q.why: Processing data and executing instructions is the wording mark schemes credit. Storing files permanently is the job of storage.

q.q: A pupil taps 'Pay' on a canteen app. Which of these is the CPU's job?
o: Keeping the app stored permanently while the phone is switched off
Carrying out the app's instructions, such as adding up the basket
Lighting up the pixels that show the receipt on the phone's screen
Holding the start-up instructions needed when the phone is turned on
q.why: The CPU processes data and executes program instructions. Storage, the screen and ROM do the other jobs.

q.q: What is the correct order of the stages the CPU repeats for each instruction?
o: Fetch, decode, execute
Decode, fetch, execute
Fetch, execute, decode
Execute, decode, fetch
q.why: An instruction must be fetched from memory before it can be decoded, and decoded before it can be executed.

q.q: Which answer about the CPU's purpose would earn credit in a GCSE exam?
o: It is the brain of the computer and is in charge of everything
It processes data and carries out the instructions of programs
It does everything that happens inside the computer system
It runs the computer and makes all the parts work properly
q.why: 'The brain of the computer' earns nothing on its own; examiners want processing data and executing instructions.

q.q: How does the CPU control the other parts of the computer?
o: It stores a copy of every device's data in its own registers permanently
It waits for each device to send it a finished result without being asked
It switches the devices on and off using the power supply unit
It sends control signals to memory and input, output and storage devices
q.why: Control signals make memory and devices act at the right time.

q.q: Roughly how often does a modern CPU repeat the fetch–execute cycle?
o: Thousands of times every second
Millions of times every minute
Billions of times every second
Once for each program that is opened
q.why: A modern CPU repeats the cycle billions of times per second; clock speeds are measured in GHz.

q.q: Which component carries out arithmetic such as adding the cost of items at a canteen till?
o: Control unit
Immediate-access store
Memory address register
ALU
q.why: The arithmetic logic unit does the arithmetic; the control unit co-ordinates but does not calculate.

q.q: Checking whether one number is greater than another is done by the…
o: control unit
immediate-access store
program counter
ALU
q.why: Comparisons are logic operations carried out in the arithmetic logic unit.

q.q: Where is the result of an ALU calculation held first, before being stored back in memory?
o: Program counter
Accumulator
Memory address register
Hard disc drive
q.why: The accumulator is a register inside the ALU that holds the latest result.

q.q: What does the immediate-access store hold?
o: Only the boot program used at start-up
Backup copies of every file on the drive
The programs and data currently in use
The settings for the CPU's clock speed
q.why: The IAS is main memory, holding the programs and data in use; they are also kept permanently on storage.

q.q: The control unit is often compared to the conductor of an orchestra. Why?
o: It does not do the calculations itself but tells every part when to act
It carries out every calculation and comparison needed by the program
It holds every program and its data at a unique numbered address
It sets the speed at which the music and sound files are played
q.why: Like a conductor, the control unit co-ordinates the other parts rather than doing the work on data.

q.q: Why does every location in the immediate-access store have a unique address?
o: So the data is kept safe when the computer is switched off
So the ALU can decode the instructions held in each location
So the CPU can go straight to the exact instruction or data it needs
So each location can be shared by several programs at once
q.why: Each address is a number that identifies one location, so the CPU can find the instruction or data directly.

q.q: A canteen program checks whether a pupil's balance is less than £2.50. Which kind of operation is this, and where is it done?
o: An arithmetic operation, done in the control unit
A logic operation, done in the ALU
A logic operation, done in the control unit
A storage operation, done in the immediate-access store
q.why: Comparisons are logic operations, and the ALU does both arithmetic and logic. They let programs make decisions.

q.q: CCEA calls the register holding the current instruction the instruction address register (IAR). What do many textbooks call it?
o: The program counter (PC)
The instruction register (IR)
The memory data register (MDR)
The memory address register (MAR)
q.why: Both names describe the same job; use CCEA's term, IAR, in the exam.

q.q: The value 180 is read from memory address 200. Where is 180 held as it arrives in the CPU?
o: Memory address register (MAR)
Program counter (PC)
Instruction address register (IAR)
Memory data register (MDR)
q.why: Data from memory arrives in the MDR; the address 200 was in the MAR.

q.q: What happens to the program counter after an instruction has been fetched?
o: It is cleared to zero
It is copied into the ALU
It stores the result of the instruction
It is incremented by 1
q.why: Incrementing the PC means it now points to the next instruction.

q.q: Why are registers much faster to use than main memory?
o: They are part of the processor itself
They are stored on the solid state drive
They are non-volatile, unlike main memory
They hold far more data than main memory
q.why: Registers are tiny stores inside the CPU, so no trip to main memory is needed.

q.q: What does the instruction address register (IAR) hold?
o: The address of the next instruction to be fetched
The instruction currently being decoded and executed
The address of the memory location being used
The result of the most recent calculation
q.why: The control unit decodes the instruction held in the IAR. The address of the next instruction is in the PC.

q.q: The instruction being executed says 'jump to address 150'. What happens to the program counter?
o: It is changed to 150
It is incremented by 150
It is copied into the MDR
It stays the same until the jump ends
q.why: Normally the PC is incremented, but a jump instruction sets the PC to the new address.

q.q: What is a register?
o: A large area of main memory that holds all of the programs currently being used
A chip on the motherboard that holds the boot program needed at switch-on
A very small, very fast memory location inside the CPU, used for one particular job
A part of the storage drive used as extra memory when the RAM becomes full
q.why: Registers are part of the processor itself, which is why they are much faster than main memory.

q.q: The CPU needs to write the value 42 into memory address 300. What do the MAR and MDR hold?
o: MAR holds 42; MDR holds 300
MAR holds 300; MDR holds 42
PC holds 300; MDR holds 42
MAR holds 300; IAR holds 42
q.why: The MAR holds where (the address 300); the MDR holds what (the data 42) on its way to memory.

q.q: A pupil writes: 'At the start of the fetch, the data is put in the MAR.' What is wrong?
o: The MAR holds the current instruction, so data must go to the IAR
Nothing is wrong, because the MAR holds both the data and its address
The MAR holds an address; data and instructions travel through the MDR
The MAR holds the result of a calculation, so data must go to the ALU
q.why: The first fetch step copies the address in the PC to the MAR. Putting data in the MAR is a common mistake.

q.q: During the decode stage, which part of the CPU works out what the instruction in the IAR means?
o: The control unit
The ALU
The MDR
The accumulator
q.why: The control unit decodes the instruction, working out the operation and the data or address needed.

q.q: The program counter holds 57 at the start of a fetch. What does it hold at the end of the fetch?
q.why: The PC is incremented by 1 during the fetch, so it points to the next instruction.

q.q: During execute, an instruction needs a value from memory. How is it read?
o: Its address goes into the MDR and the value comes back through the MAR
Its address goes into the PC and the value comes back through the IAR
Its address goes into the MAR and the value comes back through the MDR
Its address goes into the accumulator and the value comes back through the ALU
q.why: The MAR always holds the address being used, and all transfers to and from memory go through the MDR.

q.q: Which is the correct order of the fetch stage?
o: PC → MDR; memory → MAR; MAR → IAR; PC + 1
PC + 1; PC → MAR; memory → MDR; MDR → IAR
PC → MAR; memory → IAR; IAR → MDR; PC + 1
PC → MAR; memory → MDR; MDR → IAR; PC + 1
q.why: The address goes from the PC to the MAR, the instruction comes into the MDR, then into the IAR, and the PC is incremented.

q.q: After an instruction arrives in the MDR during fetch, where is it copied next?
o: The instruction address register (IAR)
The memory address register (MAR)
The program counter (PC)
The accumulator in the ALU
q.why: The instruction moves from the MDR into the IAR, where the control unit decodes it.

q.q: During execute, a result must be saved to memory. How does it get there?
o: It goes out through the MAR to the address held in the MDR
It is copied from the accumulator into the program counter
It is copied from the IAR to the address held in the PC
It goes out through the MDR to the address held in the MAR
q.why: The address to write to goes in the MAR and the data travels through the MDR.

q.q: At the start of a fetch the program counter holds 120. What do the MAR and the PC hold at the end of the fetch stage?
o: MAR 121, PC 121
MAR 120, PC 121
MAR 120, PC 120
MAR 121, PC 120
q.why: 120 is copied into the MAR to fetch that instruction, then the PC is incremented to 121.

q.q: Rendering a video is a job that splits up easily. Which change to a computer helps most with it?
o: A larger ROM chip
More virtual memory
A larger Blu-ray drive
More cores in the processor
q.why: Several cores can process parts of the job in parallel. Virtual memory on storage is slow.

q.q: A processor runs at 3.2 GHz. How many fetch–execute cycles can it carry out per second?
q.why: 1 GHz = 1,000,000,000 cycles per second, so 3.2 GHz = 3,200,000,000.

q.q: Why does a larger cache usually improve CPU performance?
o: More cycles can be carried out per second, so each instruction is fetched more quickly
More cores are added to the processor, so more instructions run at the same time
More of the operating system is stored permanently, so the computer boots faster
More frequently used data is kept close to the CPU, so there are fewer slow trips to RAM
q.why: The CPU checks the cache first; a larger cache means fewer slower RAM accesses.

q.q: Extra cores improve performance most when…
o: the computer has a larger screen attached
software can split its work to run in parallel
the ROM is larger than the RAM in the computer
only one simple program is running at a time
q.why: Each core fetches, decodes and executes its own instructions, so work must be split to benefit.

q.q: What is a core?
o: A complete processing unit with its own control unit, ALU and registers
A small amount of very fast memory found right next to the processor
The clock inside the CPU that sends out regular pulses to each part
The main memory that holds programs and data while they are in use
q.why: A multi-core processor has several of these, so it can process several instructions at the same time.

q.q: Doubling the clock speed rarely doubles a computer's overall speed. Which is a reason?
o: Other slower parts, such as RAM, can make the CPU wait
Clock speed has no effect on the number of cycles per second
A faster clock reduces the amount of cache the CPU can use
A faster clock means software can no longer use several cores
q.why: The CPU may wait for slower components; higher clock speeds also produce more heat and use more power.

q.q: Which answer would earn both marks for explaining how more cores improve performance?
o: More cores, so more instructions can be processed at the same time
More cores, so the computer is faster and quicker than before
More cores, so there is more memory to store programs in use
More cores, so each fetch–execute cycle happens more times a second
q.why: Cause and effect: more cores means instructions are processed in parallel. More cycles per second is clock speed.

q.q: Why is cache measured in megabytes when RAM is measured in gigabytes?
o: Cache only needs to hold the boot program, which is very short
Cache is part of the hard disc, which has less room for memory
Cache is built from very fast, expensive memory, so only a small amount is fitted
Cache is non-volatile, so it cannot be made as large as RAM
q.why: Faster memory is more expensive, so cache is kept small.

q.q: A pupil has a browser, an essay and a music app open. Where are they all held while in use?
o: ROM
The boot program
RAM
The storage drive only
q.why: RAM holds the operating system, programs and data currently in use. They are also saved on storage, but run from RAM.

q.q: Which pair of memories are both volatile?
o: RAM and cache
ROM and cache
RAM and ROM
ROM and SSD
q.why: RAM and cache lose their contents when the power goes off; ROM is non-volatile.

q.q: What is virtual memory?
o: Part of the storage drive used as extra RAM when RAM is full
Memory held in the cloud and reached over the internet
Another name for the ROM that holds the boot program
A small area of very fast memory found inside the ALU
q.why: When RAM fills up, the OS moves unused data to storage. Storage is much slower, so the computer slows down.

q.q: What is the purpose of ROM?
o: To hold the operating system, programs and data currently in use
To hold copies of the instructions and data that are used most often
To hold the boot program needed when the computer is switched on
To hold the user's saved files when the computer is switched off
q.why: ROM holds the start-up instructions. Saved files are kept on storage, not in ROM.

q.q: Why must you save an essay before switching the computer off?
o: ROM is read only, so the essay cannot be written into it later
RAM is volatile, so its contents are lost when the power goes off
Cache is too small to hold the essay once the power goes off
Storage is volatile, so the essay must be copied to RAM instead
q.why: While you type, the essay is in RAM, which loses everything without power; saving writes it to storage.

q.q: A slow computer often has its RAM full. Why can adding more RAM make it feel faster?
o: More RAM raises the clock speed, so more cycles are carried out per second
There is less need for virtual memory on the much slower storage drive
More RAM adds extra cores, so more programs can be run in parallel
More RAM is non-volatile, so programs do not need to be loaded again
q.why: With more RAM, less data is moved out to slow storage as virtual memory.

q.q: What does cache hold?
o: Copies of the instructions and data used most often
The boot program that runs when the computer starts
Every program and file stored on the computer
Data that has been moved out of RAM when it is full
q.why: Cache reduces the time the CPU waits for RAM. Data moved out of RAM goes to virtual memory on storage.

q.q: Where are a pupil's saved essays kept while the computer is switched off?
o: In the ROM chip on the motherboard
In the cache beside the CPU
In RAM, until it is next switched on
On the storage drive, such as an SSD or HDD
q.why: Saved files are on storage. ROM holds the boot program and cache and RAM are volatile.

q.q: Why is the boot program stored in ROM?
o: ROM is the fastest memory, so the computer starts quickly
ROM is larger than RAM, so the whole program fits in it
ROM is non-volatile, so the program is there at switch-on
ROM can be edited easily, so the program is kept up to date
q.why: RAM is empty at switch-on, so the instructions must be in non-volatile ROM.

q.q: On modern PCs, where is the firmware (often UEFI) stored so that it can be updated?
o: Cache
RAM
Flash memory
The MDR
q.why: Firmware is kept in flash memory so it can be updated, but it plays the same role as ROM at GCSE.

q.q: A computer has finished booting. What does RAM now hold?
o: Only the boot program copied from ROM
Nothing until the user saves a file
The power-on self-test results only
The operating system, programs and data in use
q.why: After boot, ROM is not normally used again and RAM holds what is in use.

q.q: Why is RAM empty when the computer is switched on?
o: It is read only, so the operating system cannot be stored in it permanently
It is cleared by the boot program to make room for the operating system
It is volatile, so it lost everything when the computer was last switched off
It is too small to hold anything until the cache has been loaded first
q.why: RAM loses its contents without power, so the CPU must get its first instructions from ROM.

q.q: What does the power-on self-test check?
o: That the user's password matches the one on the server
That every application installed is the latest version
Key hardware such as RAM, the keyboard and the storage drive
That the files on the storage drive are free of viruses
q.why: The boot program runs a power-on self-test of key hardware before loading the OS.

q.q: Which is the correct order of events at boot-up?
o: Boot program runs; hardware checked; OS found and loaded into RAM; OS takes control
Hardware checked; OS loaded into ROM; boot program runs; OS takes control
OS loaded into RAM; boot program runs; hardware checked; OS takes control
Boot program runs; OS loaded into ROM; hardware checked; login screen appears
q.why: ROM's boot program runs first, checks hardware, finds the OS on storage and copies it into RAM.

q.q: Why is it important that ROM is read only?
o: The boot program can be read faster than anything in cache
The boot program can be changed by any user who needs to
The boot program is copied into ROM each time it starts
The boot program cannot be accidentally deleted or overwritten
q.why: Read only means users and most software cannot change or delete it.

q.q: Which of these memories is non-volatile?
o: RAM
ROM
Cache
Registers
q.why: ROM keeps its contents without power; RAM, cache and registers lose theirs.

q.q: Which statement about cache is correct?
o: It is faster than RAM but has a smaller capacity
It is non-volatile, so it keeps data without power
It is part of the hard disc and stores saved files
It is read only and holds the computer's boot program
q.why: Cache is fast but small because it is expensive. It is volatile and read/write.

q.q: Which pair of memories can both be read from and written to?
o: ROM and cache
RAM and cache
RAM and ROM
ROM and registers
q.why: Only ROM is read only.

q.q: Typical RAM in a new laptop is measured in…
o: kilobytes
terabytes
gigabytes
hertz
q.why: A laptop typically has 8–32 GB of RAM.

q.q: What is a typical size for the cache in a modern CPU?
o: A few megabytes, e.g. 4–36 MB
A few gigabytes, e.g. 8–32 GB
A few terabytes, e.g. 1–4 TB
A few kilobytes, e.g. 4–36 KB
q.why: Cache is measured in megabytes; RAM is measured in gigabytes.

q.q: Which memory has the highest cost per byte?
o: RAM
Cache
ROM
Hard disc drive
q.why: Cache is built from the fastest, most expensive memory, which is why only a few megabytes are fitted.

q.q: Which shows the memory hierarchy from fastest and smallest to slowest and largest?
o: Registers, cache, RAM, storage
Cache, registers, RAM, storage
Registers, RAM, cache, storage
Storage, RAM, cache, registers
q.why: Registers are at the top of the pyramid, then cache, then RAM, with storage at the bottom.

q.q: Which answer would earn full marks for a difference between RAM and ROM?
o: RAM is volatile but ROM is non-volatile
RAM is volatile and loses its contents
ROM is non-volatile and holds the BIOS
RAM and ROM are both inside the computer
q.why: A comparison needs both sides of the point; describing only one memory gets at most half the marks.

q.q: On a touch screen, what does double-tapping act as?
o: Drag-and-drop
A double-click
A single click
Scrolling with a wheel
q.why: Tapping is a click, double-tapping is a double-click and dragging a finger is drag-and-drop.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of using a microphone for voice input?
o: Speaking is much slower than typing the same words in
Background noise reduces how accurately speech is recognised
It needs a flat surface to work on, such as a desk
It cannot be used hands-free while doing something else
q.why: Noise lowers recognition accuracy. Voice input is usually faster than typing and hands-free.

q.q: Which device is best for a designer drawing detailed artwork by hand?
o: Graphics digitiser
Mouse
Touch screen kiosk
Microphone
q.why: A pad and stylus gives natural, accurate, often pressure-sensitive drawing.

q.q: How does a touch screen work out where it was touched?
o: A camera behind the glass takes a picture of the finger and finds where it is
The touch changes the electrical signal and the position is calculated as x, y co-ordinates
The sound of the tap is picked up and timed to find which part was touched
The screen measures the heat of the finger to decide which icon was chosen
q.why: A touch changes the signal, and the position is worked out as co-ordinates.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of a graphics digitiser?
o: It is less accurate than a mouse for drawing detailed artwork
It cannot detect how hard the stylus is pressed on the pad
It is more expensive than a mouse and poor for selecting menus
It must be used with the drawing shown on the pad itself
q.why: Digitisers cost more and are not good for menus. The drawing usually appears on the monitor.

q.q: For which context is a mouse least suitable?
o: Using a laptop on a crowded train
Using an office PC at a desk
Selecting icons on a desktop
Opening a right-click menu
q.why: A mouse needs a flat surface, which a train seat does not provide.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of a touch screen on a shared fast-food kiosk?
o: The screen gets dirty, which is a hygiene issue
Customers need training before using it
It needs a separate keyboard and mouse
It cannot show pictures of the food
q.why: Touch screens need little skill, but shared screens get dirty and only a limited number of options fit.

q.q: Why does voice input need more storage than typed input?
o: Sound is stored on ROM rather than RAM
Sound must be saved twice for accuracy
Sound files are converted into images
Sound files need far more storage than text
q.why: Recording speech produces sound data, which is much larger than the equivalent text.

q.q: How does a 3D printer create an object?
o: It carves the object from a solid block of plastic
It builds the object one thin layer at a time
It prints toner onto layers of paper and folds them
It scans a real object and copies its outside shape
q.why: 3D printing is additive: the object is built layer by layer from a CAD model.

q.q: Why are laser printers good for a busy school office?
o: They can print multipart carbon-copy forms
They print large volumes quickly at high quality
Colour laser printers are cheap to buy and run
They build models and prototypes for lessons
q.why: Laser printers are fast for large runs with sharp text. Colour models are expensive and they cannot print carbon copies.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of speakers in an open-plan office?
o: They need a stylus to control the volume
They can distract other workers nearby
They can only be connected by a cable
They need toner to produce the sound
q.why: Sound carries to other people, so headphones may be better.

q.q: Which is a typical use of a 3D printer?
o: Printing 500 copies of a newsletter
Printing carbon-copy order forms
Mass-producing thousands of toys
Making a custom prosthetic hand
q.why: 3D printers suit custom one-off items and prototypes; they are not economical for mass production.

q.q: In a laser printer, what is toner?
o: Liquid ink sprayed through tiny holes onto the paper
A thin plastic layer melted to build up the page
A ribbon struck by pins to mark the paper
Powdered ink that sticks to the charged areas of the drum
q.why: Toner is powdered ink; it sticks to the charged pattern on the drum and is fused with heat.

q.q: How is the image put onto the drum of a laser printer?
o: A laser beam burns the image into the surface of the drum
Toner is sprayed through holes in the drum by the laser
The drum is heated where the laser shines, melting the toner
A laser beam draws it as a pattern of static electric charge
q.why: The charge pattern attracts toner, which is then transferred to paper and fused with heat.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of a 3D printer?
o: It cannot make custom one-off objects such as prosthetic hands
It can only print in plastic and never in metal or ceramics
It can only print flat 2D designs on sheets of paper or card
It is slow for large objects and not economical for mass production
q.why: One-off items are cheap and quick, but large objects take a long time and mass production is uneconomical.

q.q: Which storage device has no moving parts?
o: HDD
Blu-ray drive
SSD
DVD drive
q.why: SSDs store data on flash memory chips.

q.q: What is the main advantage of an HDD over an SSD?
o: Faster access to files
Better at surviving knocks
Lower cost per gigabyte
Silent and lighter
q.why: HDDs give large capacity cheaply. SSDs are faster, more durable and silent.

q.q: Why can a Blu-ray disc hold more data than a DVD of the same size?
o: Its red laser makes larger pits that can each hold more data
It stores data on magnetic tracks rather than as pits and lands
It contains flash memory chips under its protective coating
Its blue-violet laser makes smaller pits that are packed more tightly
q.why: The shorter-wavelength blue-violet laser gives a smaller beam, so more pits fit on the disc.

q.q: Which storage technology does a hard disc drive use?
o: Magnetic
Flash
Optical
Volatile
q.why: An HDD stores data magnetically on spinning platters. SSDs use flash and Blu-ray is optical.

q.q: How much data does a single-layer Blu-ray disc hold?
o: 50 GB
25 GB
4.7 GB
2 TB
q.why: Single layer holds 25 GB and dual layer 50 GB; a single-layer DVD holds 4.7 GB.

q.q: A laptop with an SSD boots and opens files much faster than one with an HDD. Why?
o: The SSD is volatile, so the operating system is already in it at switch-on
The SSD has no moving parts, so it does not wait for platters to spin and heads to move
The SSD stores data magnetically, which is faster than flash memory chips
The SSD holds the boot program, so it does not need ROM at all at start-up
q.why: With no moving parts, flash storage gives much faster access than a spinning disc.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of an SSD?
o: It is easily damaged if the laptop is dropped while it runs
It is noisier than an HDD because of its spinning platters
Each memory cell can only be rewritten a limited number of times
It loses all of its data as soon as the power is turned off
q.why: SSDs cost more per GB and cells wear out after many rewrites. They are durable, silent and non-volatile.

q.q: Why are HDDs more likely than SSDs to be damaged if dropped?
o: They store data in flash memory chips that crack easily when hit
They have moving parts, such as heads on an arm over spinning platters
They use a laser that can be knocked out of line by a fall
They are volatile, so a knock can make them lose their data
q.why: Moving parts can wear out or be damaged. SSDs have none.

q.q: Why is a USB flash drive described as 'plug and play'?
o: It can play music and videos as soon as it is plugged in
It needs no power from the computer to store or read data
It has moving parts that start spinning when it is plugged in
It works as soon as it is plugged in, without installing a driver
q.why: The computer recognises it straight away.

q.q: Which device would add extra storage to a digital camera?
o: Smart card
Hard disc drive
Memory card
ROM chip
q.why: SD or microSD cards add storage to cameras, phones and drones.

q.q: What is the main job of a phone's SIM card?
o: Storing the phone's photos and videos
Holding the phone's boot program
Holding the subscriber's identity for the network
Adding extra storage space for apps
q.why: A SIM is a smart card whose main job is identity, not storing your files. Photos go on a memory card or internal storage.

q.q: What do USB flash drives, memory cards and smart cards have in common?
o: They all use magnetic platters to store data
They all use flash memory with no moving parts
They all use volatile memory chips to store data
They all use a laser to read optical pits
q.why: They are all solid state: non-volatile, compact and tough.

q.q: What is the main risk of carrying coursework on an unencrypted USB flash drive?
o: It has moving parts that break when carried in a school bag
It loses its data when it is unplugged from the computer
It is easy to lose, and anyone who finds it can read the data
It needs a special driver installed on every school computer
q.why: USB drives are small and easily lost, so unencrypted data can be read by a finder.

q.q: Which typical capacity best matches a smart card?
o: Tens of gigabytes
Hundreds of gigabytes
A few kilobytes
Several terabytes
q.why: Smart cards store only a small amount of data, such as identity or account details.

q.q: A photographer works outdoors in all weathers and often drops kit. Which criterion matters most when choosing storage?
o: Capacity
Cost per gigabyte
Access speed
Durability
q.why: Durability is how well a device survives knocks and wear, the key need for someone working outdoors.

q.q: Which criterion describes how well a storage device survives being dropped?
o: Capacity
Portability
Access speed
Durability
q.why: Durability is how well a device survives knocks and wear; portability is how easy it is to carry.

q.q: Which storage device has the fastest access speed?
o: HDD
SSD
Blu-ray
USB flash drive
q.why: SSDs are fastest because flash has no moving parts. Blu-ray is slowest.

q.q: Which of these points is comparative?
o: An SSD has fast access to its files
An HDD is a cheap form of storage
A Blu-ray disc is an optical disc
An SSD has faster access than an HDD
q.why: A comparative point compares two devices using words like 'faster than'.

q.q: A film company wants to sell copies of an HD film in shops cheaply. Which storage is most suitable?
o: SSDs
External HDDs
Smart cards
Blu-ray discs
q.why: Blu-ray discs are cheap to mass-produce and store HD films without loss of quality.

q.q: Which statement about comparing storage devices is correct?
o: SSDs win on every criterion, so they are always the best recommendation
HDDs win on every criterion except portability, so they are usually best
No device wins on every criterion, so the best choice depends on the scenario
Blu-ray wins on capacity and cost, so it is best for most backups
q.why: Each device wins on some criteria and loses on others.

q.q: A pupil only uses a laptop for word processing and browsing. Which advice is best?
o: A modest specification is enough and costs less
An 8-core processor is needed to type essays
At least 32 GB of RAM is needed for browsing
A large cache is needed to store documents
q.why: Powerful specifications suit tasks like video editing; for simple tasks a cheaper, modest specification is enough.

q.q: Which justification would earn the most credit for a touch screen in a museum kiosk?
o: Touch screens are modern and make the museum look up to date
Touch screens are better than other devices for this kind of job
Visitors need no training – they just tap the exhibit they want
A touch screen is an output device as well as an input device
q.why: A justification links the feature to the users and the context.

q.q: A rugby club wants to back up 4 TB of match videos as cheaply as possible. What is the best choice?
o: External HDD
Blu-ray discs
External SSD
USB flash drives
q.why: An HDD gives large capacity at the lowest cost per GB. 4 TB would need many Blu-ray discs.

q.q: Which is the best structure for a recommendation in a hardware scenario question?
o: Device + price + the name of the manufacturer
Feature + a list of every other device available
Device + the statement that it is better than others
Device + feature + why it matters in this scenario
q.why: This structure earns the justification marks.

q.q: Which is the strongest justification for 16 GB of RAM in a video-editing computer?
o: More RAM raises the clock speed so editing is faster
RAM is non-volatile so the video files are always safe
More RAM means the computer is better than other ones
Large video files stay in RAM instead of slow virtual memory
q.why: It links the feature (more RAM) to the task (large files) and explains the effect.
